body: Patterns from Yes Bank, Credit Suisse, GE, Jet Airways, Future Retail, PC Jeweller, Zee, Reliance Capital, Paytm, Evergrande: (1) Low P/B in a lender with understated NPAs -- book value is fictional (Yes Bank divergence; CS at 0.2x TBV); (2) Low P/E on low-quality earnings -- receivable factoring, contract assets, non-GAAP adjustments (GE, Valeant); (3) Dividend yield funded by debt -- dividend > FCF (GE 2017, Evergrande); (4) 'Asset value' that needs a buyer: land banks, brands, airline slots, spectrum (Unitech, Kingfisher brand collateral, RCom spectrum) -- in distress, asset values fall with the company; (5) Promoter-levered good business -- great franchise, bad stock while pledges overhang (Zee); (6) Equity ahead of a restructuring -- debt converts, lenders or IBC wipe equity (Jet, Future, RCap, DHFL); (7) Structural decline mistaken for cyclical trough (print media, legacy telecom); (8) Post-IPO decline in insider-sold story stocks -- 'it's 70% off' is not cheap if it was 5x overpriced (Paytm). Tests: is FCF positive and covering dividends? Is debt falling? Is the 'asset' saleable today at book? Is the promoter unlevered? Piotroski F >= 7 and Z > 2.99 for value buys; else require a dated catalyst. Counter-example: genuine turnarounds (e.g., Suzlon after deleveraging) needed debt actually extinguished, not promised.

data.tests: FCF covers dividend; debt falling; F>=7; Z>2.99; promoter unpledged; asset saleable at book

title: Value-trap patterns: why 'cheap' kept getting cheaper

body: Case outcomes: confirmed frauds -- Luckin (Muddy Waters, admitted within ~2 months), Nikola (Hindenburg, founder convicted), Wirecard (FT/Zatarra/shorts, 5 years early; regulator attacked the shorts), Valeant (Citron, -90%), Enron (Chanos), Lehman (Einhorn). Contested -- Adani (Hindenburg 2023: -60% to -70% drawdowns, partial recovery, SEBI Sep 2025 closed RPT allegations without penalty; other matters pending; Hindenburg closed Jan 2025). Practical rules: (1) Evaluate the evidence type -- primary documents, store counts, registries and ex-employee testimony (Luckin, Nikola) are stronger than valuation arguments; (2) Management response quality: point-by-point rebuttal with documents vs attacks on the messenger (Wirecard, Valeant called reports 'manipulation'); (3) Independent auditor/special audit outcome (KPMG at Wirecard could not verify); (4) Even when not fraud, fragile balance sheets and stretched valuations produce big drawdowns (Adani); (5) Regulators defending a 'national champion' is not evidence. Base rates: academic studies of activist short reports generally find large negative announcement returns that persist on average (exact magnitudes vary; unverified here). For a long-only holder: on a credible report, cut to a size you can hold through a 60% fall, then wait for independent verification.

data.rule: On a credible report: size down to survivable, await independent audit/regulator
